analysis.one_liner: Increases criminal penalties for using force or threats to block someone from renting or buying a home because of who they are.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in October 1990, the bill never left a House Judiciary subcommittee and died when the Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stiffen federal criminal penalties for people who use force, threats, fire, or guns to intimidate someone out of renting, buying, or occupying a home because of their race, religion, sex, disability, national origin, or family status. Fines would rise to as much as $250,000 and prison terms to as much as 10 years, with life imprisonment where the act kills someone [S2] [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Civil and Constitutional Rights subcommittee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended [S5] [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: People who face violence or intimidation when trying to rent or buy a home because of their race, color, religion, sex, disability, national origin, or family status — and their neighbors and advocates, whom the bill also protects when they encourage or assist fair housing participation [S3]. The bill protects the underlying right to fair housing by making force and threats against it a more seriously punished federal crime [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the top fine for intimidating someone out of housing from the prior low level to $100,000 (up to 1 year in prison), and to $250,000 and up to 10 years where the act causes bodily injury [S2] [S3].

Sets a mandatory higher penalty — up to $250,000 and 5 years — for violations involving more than $100 in property damage, the use or attempted use of fire, or use or carrying of a firearm, which is how many fair-housing attacks (arson, vandalism, armed threats) actually occur [S2] [S3].
Allows imprisonment 'for any term of years or for life' when an act of housing intimidation results in death [S3].
Protects not only home-seekers but also citizens who lawfully aid or encourage others to exercise fair-housing rights, or who peacefully speak out against discrimination [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The people who commit these acts: fines of up to $250,000 and prison terms of up to 10 years, or life where someone is killed. Federal prosecutors, courts, and prisons bear the (modest) cost of enforcing the tougher penalties.

drawbacks.text: The bill's remedy is longer sentences and bigger fines, which deter and punish but do not themselves provide housing, compensation to victims, or enforcement resources — critics of penalty-enhancement bills argue heavier sentences have limited effect without active federal prosecution [S3].

It expands federal criminal law and prison exposure, including life imprisonment, which carries the standard costs and concerns of tough-on-crime legislation such as longer incarceration and greater federal involvement in local hate-crime matters [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but narrow: the bill would matter most to the relatively small number of people who face arson, armed threats, or vandalism aimed at driving them from a home because of who they are, and it gives federal prosecutors meaningful penalties for those attacks. The costs — longer prison terms and expanded federal criminal jurisdiction — are the ordinary trade-offs of any penalty increase. It is a targeted fix rather than a broad housing policy.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its civil rights subcommittee for the last three months of the Congress and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 5, 1990 by Rep. Sensenbrenner, a Republican, with six cosponsors from both parties [S3] [S4].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On October 10, 1990 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights, where it stayed [S5].
No further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill died in subcommittee [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome leaves the existing penalty structure untouched, so the practical beneficiaries are anyone who relies on intimidation, arson, or firearms to keep people out of homes, who continues to face only the old, lower penalties. No other group gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died

for.role: Original cosponsors (2 of 257 House Democrats, 4 of 175 House Republicans)

against.name: House Judiciary Committee and its Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights

against.name: End of the 101st Congress
against.what_they_did: Killed all pending bills not passed, including this one

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no opposition at all — no votes, no floor debate — only bipartisan introduction (2 of 257 House Democrats and 4 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored) and inaction in committee, so no partisan split is observable.

industries.industry: People who use force, arson, or firearms to block fair housing (including discriminatory landlords, sellers, or harassers)
industries.note: The bill raises their criminal exposure from small fines to as much as $250,000 and 5–10 years in prison, or life where someone dies. This is the only concentrated interest the bill touches.
